definition: Truly what it appears to be; real
example: Her genuine interest in the project made everyone want to help her.
origin: From Latin genuinus, meaning native or natural, from the root of gignere, to beget.

definition: Unwilling and hesitant to do something
example: He was reluctant to lend his car to a friend he barely knew.
origin: From Latin reluctari, to struggle against, from re- (against) and luctari (to struggle).

definition: Producing strong, clear images in the mind
example: I still have a vivid memory of my first day at school.
origin: From Latin vividus, meaning lively or full of life, from vivere, to live.

definition: So slight or delicate it is hard to notice
example: There was a subtle hint of lemon in the sauce that I loved.
origin: From Old French sotil, from Latin subtilis, meaning fine, thin or finely woven.

definition: Honest and direct, even when it is uncomfortable
example: In a candid interview, the actor admitted he had nearly quit the film.
origin: From Latin candidus, meaning white or pure, from candere, to shine.

definition: To grow or develop well and successfully
example: Some plants thrive in shade and barely need any direct sunlight.
origin: From Old Norse thrifask, meaning to grasp for oneself or to prosper.

definition: To make progress slow or difficult
example: Heavy snow hindered the rescue team as they climbed toward the cabin.
origin: From Old English hindrian, meaning to harm or hold back, related to the word behind.

definition: Not well known or hard to understand
example: She loves quoting obscure poets that nobody else in the class has read.
origin: From Latin obscurus, meaning dark or dim.

definition: Seeming reasonable and likely to be true
example: His excuse sounded plausible, so the teacher let him hand it in late.
origin: From Latin plausibilis, meaning deserving applause, from plaudere, to applaud.

definition: Long, slow and boring to do
example: Entering all the receipts by hand was a tedious job that took hours.
origin: From Late Latin taediosus, from Latin taedium, meaning weariness or disgust.

definition: Sudden and unexpected, often unpleasantly so
example: The meeting came to an abrupt end when the fire alarm went off.
origin: From Latin abruptus, meaning broken off, from ab- (off) and rumpere (to break).

definition: Clear, logical and easy to follow
example: After a strong coffee she finally managed to give a coherent answer.
origin: From Latin cohaerere, to stick together, from co- (together) and haerere (to stick).

definition: Working carefully and with steady effort
example: A diligent student, he reviewed his notes every evening before dinner.
origin: From Latin diligens, meaning attentive, from diligere, to value highly or love.

definition: Wanting very much to do or have something
example: The children were eager to open their presents before breakfast.
origin: From Old French aigre, meaning sharp or sour, from Latin acer, sharp.

definition: Careful to spend very little money
example: My frugal aunt reuses wrapping paper and never buys anything at full price.
origin: From Latin frugalis, meaning thrifty, from frux, fruit or value.

definition: Unfriendly and showing strong dislike or opposition
example: The crowd turned hostile when the referee cancelled the winning goal.
origin: From Latin hostilis, from hostis, meaning enemy.

definition: Not thinking you are better than others
example: Despite winning three championships, she remained humble and thanked her teammates first.
origin: From Old French, from Latin humilis, meaning low or lowly, from humus, ground.

definition: Clearly expressed and easy to understand
example: Her lucid explanation made the tax rules seem almost simple.
origin: From Latin lucidus, meaning bright or clear, from lux, light.

definition: Ordinary and dull; part of everyday life
example: He listens to podcasts to get through mundane chores like folding laundry.
origin: From Latin mundanus, meaning of the world, from mundus, world.

definition: New and unlike anything seen before
example: The engineers found a novel way to cool the battery without fans.
origin: From Old French novel, from Latin novellus, a diminutive of novus, meaning new.

definition: Acting with care and thought for the future
example: It would be prudent to save some money before quitting your job.
origin: From Latin prudens, a shortened form of providens, meaning foreseeing.

definition: Stiff and unable to bend or change
example: The school has rigid rules about phones that students find frustrating.
origin: From Latin rigidus, meaning stiff, from rigere, to be stiff.

definition: Strong, healthy and unlikely to break or fail
example: We need a robust backup system that keeps working during power cuts.
origin: From Latin robustus, meaning strong like oak, from robur, oak or strength.

definition: Hard to find because there is very little
example: Fresh water became scarce after three months without any rain.
origin: From Old North French escars, from a Vulgar Latin form of Latin excerpere, to pluck out.

definition: Honestly meaning what you say and feel
example: He offered a sincere apology and promised it would not happen again.
origin: From Latin sincerus, meaning pure, clean or whole.

definition: Nervous, strained and unable to relax
example: Everyone in the waiting room was tense as the results were announced.
origin: From Latin tensus, the past participle of tendere, meaning to stretch.

definition: Not clear, exact or fully explained
example: She gave only a vague answer when I asked where she had been.
origin: From Latin vagus, meaning wandering or uncertain.

definition: Very tired after long effort or strain
example: The weary hikers dropped their packs and collapsed beside the campfire.
origin: From Old English werig, meaning tired.

definition: Clever and funny with words
example: Her witty replies on the panel show had the whole audience laughing.
origin: From Old English wittig, meaning wise or clever, from witt, understanding or mind.

definition: Willing to take risks; brave and confident
example: Leaving a secure job to start a bakery was a bold move.
origin: From Old English beald, meaning brave or confident.

definition: Cold, empty and offering little hope
example: The job market looked bleak for graduates during the recession.
origin: From Old Norse bleikr, meaning pale or white.

definition: Quick, energetic and full of life
example: We took a brisk walk around the lake to warm up before lunch.
origin: Of uncertain origin.

definition: To force someone to do something
example: The new law compels companies to report any data breach within three days.
origin: From Latin compellere, to drive together, from com- (together) and pellere (to drive).

definition: Saying a lot clearly in few words
example: Keep your cover letter concise so the recruiter actually reads all of it.
origin: From Latin concisus, meaning cut up or brief, from com- and caedere, to cut.

definition: To discourage someone from doing something
example: Bright lights around the house can deter burglars from trying the doors.
origin: From Latin deterrere, to frighten away, from de- (away) and terrere (to frighten).

definition: To suffer something difficult patiently for a long time
example: The villagers endured months of flooding before help finally arrived.
origin: From Old French endurer, from Latin indurare, to harden, from durus, hard.

definition: To encourage something to grow or develop
example: Good managers foster trust by listening to their teams and keeping promises.
origin: From Old English fostrian, to nourish, from fostor, meaning food.

definition: To take firm hold of or fully understand
example: It took me a while to grasp how the new software actually works.
origin: From Middle English graspen, to reach for or grope, related to Old English grapian, to touch.

definition: Done too quickly and without enough thought
example: Don't make a hasty decision about the house; sleep on it first.
origin: From Old French hastif, from haste, meaning urgency, a word of Germanic origin.

definition: Not strict when punishing or enforcing rules
example: The judge was lenient because it was the teenager's first offense.
origin: From Latin leniens, from lenire, to soften, from lenis, mild or gentle.

definition: Very small in amount; barely enough
example: They survived the winter on a meager supply of rice and beans.
origin: From Old French maigre, meaning thin, from Latin macer, lean.

definition: Too trusting because of little life experience
example: I was naive enough to believe the email promising me free money.
origin: From French naïve, from Latin nativus, meaning native or natural.

definition: An idea, belief or impression about something
example: She rejected the notion that success depends only on talent.
origin: From Latin notio, meaning concept or idea, from noscere, to come to know.

definition: To leave something out, by choice or mistake
example: Please don't omit your phone number when you fill in the form.
origin: From Latin omittere, to let go, from ob- and mittere, to send.

definition: To think about something carefully and at length
example: He sat by the window and pondered whether to accept the offer.
origin: From Latin ponderare, to weigh, from pondus, meaning weight.

definition: Charming in an unusual, old-fashioned way
example: We stayed in a quaint fishing village with cobbled streets and tiny shops.
origin: From Old French cointe, meaning clever or pretty, from Latin cognitus, known.

definition: To prove that a claim is wrong
example: The lawyer used phone records to refute the witness's version of events.
origin: From Latin refutare, meaning to drive back or rebut.

definition: Calm, peaceful and completely untroubled
example: The lake was serene at dawn, without a single ripple on the water.
origin: From Latin serenus, meaning clear or calm, first said of the sky and weather.

definition: Doubting that something is true or useful
example: Doctors were skeptical about the diet until the trial results came in.
origin: From Greek skeptikos, meaning inquiring, from skeptesthai, to look or consider.

definition: Refusing to change your mind or give way
example: My stubborn grandfather still refuses to use a mobile phone.
origin: Of uncertain origin.

definition: Strongly built and not easily damaged
example: You will need sturdy boots for a trail this rocky and steep.
origin: From Old French estourdi, meaning dazed or reckless; the sense of strongly built came later in English.
